1GcVa4jFySlun4jLSuMhiq: Keith Richards said once that the name came from his baby daughter, Angela. Then, years later, in his book, he said no, he'd picked it before he even knew the baby would be a girl, and the song isn't about anybody. That hasn't stopped half the world guessing. I don't guess. I listen to how tired Jagger sounds, like a man who's been saying goodbye for weeks and still hasn't left the room. Nicky Hopkins on the piano, holding the whole thing up. [quietly] There's a hairband on my shelf I keep meaning to post back. This doesn't help. Angie, The Rolling Stones.
5gz38AxRkD6Ywxd4fr2pLj: Thom Yorke said they spent a whole day going round in circles on this, and then it came together all at once. He'd been reading a Ben Okri novel, The Famished Road, and listening to a lot of R.E.M., and if you know both you can hear them in it. What I hear is that guitar figure he wrote, Ed O'Brien playing it, turning over and over with Jonny's line on top. It's the sound the anchor chain makes when the boat swings: the same few notes, round and round. Most people find it the saddest thing they own. I find it a comfort. Radiohead, Street Spirit.
7BZLNqU7zChzcnSo6ETJ5l: Paul Heaton wrote the words to this sitting in a bar on the Lijnbaan in Rotterdam, while the staff were doing their best to get him to leave. He called it a bitchy song himself, and it is, though Jacqui Abbott sings it so sweetly you nearly miss the teeth. The idea is that every town's the same once you're standing in it. Eleven years I went back and forth to one harbour on the ferry, and I won't pretend that didn't feel true some weeks. [dryly] Being sacked fixed it. Rotterdam, or Anywhere, The Beautiful South.
5MxNLUsfh7uzROypsoO5qe: Steven Tyler's father played classical piano, and Tyler says he used to lie underneath it as a small boy, listening. That's where he got these chords, he reckons. He worked the song out on an old upright years before Aerosmith even existed. The first time it came out it hardly sold, except around Boston. A couple of years later they released it a second time, and it went into the American top ten. I like a song that waits on the shelf until everybody catches up with it. [wistful] I've got a few things in my life I'm hoping work the same way. Dream On, by Aerosmith.
3yO1OjqT59JyjHaQZcCYDX: Chris Frantz, the drummer, had just been to see Parliament-Funkadelic, and the crowd there had a chant he couldn't get out of his head, so at the next jam he kept shouting it. David Byrne liked it, made it the title, and then sang nonsense sounds over the groove until real words fitted the shapes. That's why the lines don't add up to a story, and why it doesn't matter one bit. It was their only top ten hit in America. Living on an old boat with a generator that coughs, I play it purely as music, you understand. Talking Heads, Burning Down the House.
5eSllZgRWCIJsDTAqFRwQw: Damon Albarn couldn't finish this one, so Graham Coxon took it over, wrote the words and sang it himself. It's about him giving up the drink: staying in with coffee and the telly instead of the pub, and wanting out of the life he'd got stuck in. In the video a little milk carton goes looking for him, because his face is printed on the side as missing. I've always liked that it's the quiet one in the band who got the song everybody hums. When I first came out here I drank more coffee than was wise and talked to the gull more than was healthy. Both still true. Blur, Coffee and TV.
1vP2JEXRsGrFbwOZ0foOQ5: Bowie made this in France and finished it in Berlin, trying to pull himself out of some very bad years. He called it his ultimate retreat song: a man alone in a blue room with the blinds down, waiting for something to arrive. Brian Eno had Mary Hopkin sing her bits before there were even any words, and Eno wanted the voice held back, to throw you, so the band goes on a long while before Bowie turns up. Sad words on a happy tune, which is how most people get through a bad patch. [quietly] I had a retreat as well. Mine floats. David Bowie, Sound and Vision.
0I3q5fE6wg7LIfHGngUTnV: André 3000 started this at home on an acoustic guitar, of all things, before it grew into what you know. It's partly about Erykah Badu, the mother of his son, and partly about her mother. Badu said it stung at first, and then she found it honest. And her mother? Loved it so much she had a number plate made with the song's name on it. I don't think a song can get a better review than that. I once sat across a kitchen table from a mother like that for two hours, and nobody made a number plate about me. [dryly] Probably for the best. Outkast, Ms. Jackson.
0j3p1p06deJ7f9xmJ9yG22: Paul McCartney had Chuck Berry's Back in the U.S.A. in mind and turned it round: not an American glad to be home, but a Russian. He was playing it on an acoustic guitar in India when Mike Love of the Beach Boys told him the middle should be about the girls, and you can hear exactly where he took the advice. The plane at the start is an old turboprop from the studio's library of sounds. I like a song about being glad to get home. Every supply run, coming back in the dinghy with the coffee, the boat gets bigger and I get happier, and Gerrit doesn't even look up. The Beatles, Back in the U.S.S.R.
5UWwZ5lm5PKu6eKsHAGxOk: Dave Grohl wrote most of this in about three quarters of an hour, in the middle of a divorce, sleeping on a friend's floor. It's about Louise Post from Veruca Salt, who he'd fallen for, and she sang her part down a telephone line from Chicago. Grohl played the drums himself; there was no drummer in the band just then. The talking you hear in the quiet bit is the engineer telling a story from when he was a boy. I did five months on Henk's sofa once. He hid the biscuits. I didn't write anything like this. Everlong, Foo Fighters.
5uvosCdMlFdTXhoazkTI5R: Jim Morrison told the others to go away and write songs, and Robby Krieger asked what about. Something universal, Morrison said, something that wouldn't go out of style. So Krieger thought of earth, air, fire and water, and took fire, partly because he liked the Stones' Play With Fire. Morrison added the second verse. Later a television show asked them to change one word, about getting higher, and Morrison sang it as written, live, and they were never asked back. [deadpan] I know a bit about never being asked back. A ferry company has my name on a list. The Doors, Light My Fire.
6kopmMZiyLmw7h66uXcXR7: Dave McCabe of the Zutons wrote this in the back of a taxi, in about twenty minutes, and he said the whole thing was done before he got where he was going. It's for a friend of his in America who'd got in trouble with the law over her driving, and it's really a postcard: I'm not doing so well, come over and see me. Years later she was named, a make-up artist called Valerie Star. That's what gets me. All those people singing it in pubs, and it was one letter to one person. The letters I get come in bottles, and nobody ever signs them. Mark Ronson and Amy Winehouse, Valerie.
6jwE5S7xZ4G2CiisKz7NM1: The voices in this come off a gospel record from nineteen forty-nine, Bill Landford and the Landfordaires, singing an old hymn. The hymn says you can run as far as you like, and what's coming for you will still get there. Moby said this was a hard one to put together, all done on samplers, not a computer, bit by bit. I like that a song half a century old can turn up and sound like it's in a hurry. I ran a fair way myself, as it happens. Out past the line, onto a boat. The letters still found me. Run On, Moby.
2BkXpZSvPoUDMLI2Xw9kAL: The idea came from a conversation in Denmark, John Lennon and Yoko Ono with her ex-husband and his new partner, about karma that doesn't wait for your next life, but gets you straight away. Phil Spector produced it, George Harrison's on guitar, Billy Preston on the organ, and it was the first record by a Beatle on his own to sell a million in America. When Lennon went on Top of the Pops with it, he'd just had all his hair cropped short. I did mine once with the kitchen scissors in the wheelhouse window. Karma came instantly. Gerrit took one look and flew off. Instant Karma, John Lennon.
59WN2psjkt1tyaxjspN8fp: Tom Morello was teaching a guitar student a different way of tuning when this riff fell out of him. He stopped the lesson to put it on tape, and the band built the song the next day. It's about police violence and who the police are really there for, and it came out of Los Angeles at a time when that was not an abstract question. In nineteen ninety-three a DJ on the BBC played the uncut version by mistake, in the middle of the chart show, and they had a hundred and thirty-eight complaints. [mock-serious] I'd be delighted with that many listeners. Rage Against the Machine, Killing in the Name.
5Xak5fmy089t0FYmh3VJiY: Stone Gossard had the music first, an instrumental he just called E Ballad, and Eddie Vedder put the words on it: a first love, and having to let it go. When the album took off, the record company wanted it out as a single, and the band said no. Vedder said fragile songs get crushed by the business, and I think he was right to keep it back. Out here nobody's in charge of what gets crushed. I play it when I need it, and not too often, so it stays what it is. [quietly] Some records you hold by the edges. Pearl Jam, Black.
5veJDT0MLsLbhYsx42GXUD: Sting was an English teacher before The Police, and this is a teacher, a girl in his class, and the guilt and fear when the whole school starts to notice. There's a line in it that names Nabokov, the man who wrote Lolita, and the critics had a field day with the rhyme. Sting admitted it was clumsy. It still sold more than anything else in Britain that year. I only ever had one teacher who frightened me, a woman who taught geography and could hear you thinking. I learned where every port in Europe was. Turned out useful. Don't Stand So Close To Me, The Police.
4xlEKYv7HmC8zXoJIbpZKM: First song Jack White and Brendan Benson ever wrote together. They lived three streets apart in Detroit, and Benson had a slow reggae demo with only one verse. White took it from there. He said it's asking whether getting married and settling down is starting a new life or giving up on the old one. I came close to settled, once. A flat, a boiler that worked half the time, somebody who knew where everything was. Then one lap of the harbour, and here I am, settled on an anchor instead. I still don't know the answer to his question. Steady, As She Goes, The Raconteurs.
26QKxvjlCo2fSd3T4c8Zpb: Neil Young had a bad back when he wrote this, couldn't stand for long, so he sat down with an acoustic guitar instead of an electric one. They recorded it in Nashville, and James Taylor and Linda Ronstadt happened to be in town for Johnny Cash's television show, so they sang on it. It's his only number one in America. Bob Dylan said he didn't like hearing it, because it sounded like him. Young said it put him in the middle of the road, so he headed for the ditch. I have one chair on this boat. The whole station is done sitting down. Heart of Gold, Neil Young.
2fXKyAyPrEa24c6PJyqznF: Jarvis Cocker met a Greek girl at art college, a sculpture student, who told him she wanted to move to Hackney and live like the common people. He doesn't even know her name. He wrote the tune on a cheap little Casio keyboard, the band mostly shrugged, and only Candida Doyle heard what it was. It's about rich people playing at being poor, which they can stop doing any time they like. [dryly] Ruud and I went abroad to pick peaches once, for the adventure. He lasted four days and went home with my sleeping bag. I stayed. Pulp, Common People.
5OWsea313ovaQoXvsgWq79: Noel Gallagher wrote this between the first two albums, and they did the strings with a proper session orchestra, one of them an old fiddle player from the Electric Light Orchestra. Then somebody noticed it borrowed a bit from How Sweet to Be an Idiot, a song by Neil Innes, and it was settled out of court, so Innes has his name on it now and a share of the money. He made a joke about it later on a Rutles record, which is the right way to win an argument. The keeper's copy came over in the fruit crate with a bus ticket in the sleeve. I've left it there. Whatever, by Oasis.
5DiXcVovI0FcY2s0icWWUu: Adam Duritz and his mate Marty Jones went to see Marty's father play flamenco guitar, and afterwards they went to a bar. A drummer from some band was in there with three women round him, and the two of them, who couldn't talk to a girl to save their lives, decided being rock stars would sort it out. Duritz went home and wrote this. Later he said it was really about himself, and for a while he'd only play it slow, or not at all. I drove the van for a band once that thought the same thing. Nobody ever heard of them. Mr. Jones, Counting Crows.
